WORKPLACE LANGUAGE RESTRICTION POLICY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Government Code section 12951, a Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) provision that limits when Acme, Inc. may adopt or enforce a workplace policy restricting which language Jordan Lee, in the position of Retail Sales Associate, may use on the job. It states facts about what the statute requires, permits, and defines -- the two conditions a language restriction must satisfy, the statute's own definition of "business necessity," and which employers the statute covers -- and it compares the statute to a related, though not identical, federal EEOC guideline on the same subject. This document is informational: it does not evaluate whether any specific policy at Acme, Inc. complies with section 12951, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee what to do about any particular language-related workplace rule.

RESTRICTING LANGUAGE USE IS AN UNLAWFUL EMPLOYMENT PRACTICE UNLESS TWO CONDITIONS ARE MET
California Government Code section 12951(a) states that it is an unlawful employment practice for an employer, as FEHA defines that term, to adopt or enforce a policy that limits or prohibits the use of any language in any workplace, unless both of two conditions the statute itself lists are satisfied. The prohibition is written broadly -- it reaches a policy that "limits or prohibits the use of any language," not only a policy that bans a specific named language -- and it applies to "any workplace," without the statute's own text distinguishing by industry, job duties, or the size of the restriction. The statute's two conditions, addressed in separate clauses of this document, are that the restriction be justified by a business necessity and that the employer have given employees a specific kind of notice about it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 12926, to adopt or enforce a policy that limits or prohibits the use of any language in any workplace, unless both of the following conditions exist:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12951(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12951(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12951.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that any specific policy at any specific workplace does or does not violate this section. The statute's text does not itself define "workplace" or "any language," and this clause does not attempt to resolve, for example, whether the statute reaches a policy limited to a single work area, a single shift, or written communications as opposed to spoken ones -- no case law construing those terms was located or verified in this research session. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 12951(a); the two conditions it refers to are addressed with their own citations in separate clauses below rather than repeated here.

FIRST CONDITION: THE RESTRICTION MUST BE JUSTIFIED BY A BUSINESS NECESSITY
The first of section 12951(a)'s two conditions is that the language restriction be justified by a business necessity. The statute states this as a one-sentence requirement and separately defines what "business necessity" means for purposes of the section, in the companion clause of the same statute addressed elsewhere in this document. By the statute's own structure, this condition and the notice condition addressed in the next clause are both required -- the statute's introductory sentence uses the word "both," not "either."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) The language restriction is justified by a business necessity."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12951(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12951(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12951.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory paragraph, section 12951(a)(1); it does not restate the statute's own definition of "business necessity," which appears in a separate clause below quoting subdivision (b). This clause does not determine whether any specific reason an employer might give for a language restriction meets this statutory standard -- that is a fact-specific inquiry the statute's own text leaves to be applied to particular circumstances, and no case law applying it was located or verified in this research session. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

"BUSINESS NECESSITY" IS DEFINED BY THE STATUTE ITSELF, IN THREE PARTS
Government Code section 12951(b) defines "business necessity," for purposes of the section, as an overriding legitimate business purpose such that three things are all true: the language restriction is necessary to the safe and efficient operation of the business; the language restriction effectively fulfills the business purpose it is supposed to serve; and there is no alternative practice to the language restriction that would accomplish the business purpose equally well with a lesser discriminatory impact. By its own terms, the definition combines a necessity requirement, an effectiveness requirement, and a least-discriminatory-alternative requirement -- it does not treat a restriction as justified merely because the employer can articulate some legitimate business reason for it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) For the purposes of this section, “business necessity” means an overriding legitimate business purpose such that the language restriction is necessary to the safe and efficient operation of the business, that the language restriction effectively fulfills the business purpose it is supposed to serve, and there is no alternative practice to the language restriction that would accomplish the business purpose equally well with a lesser discriminatory impact."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12951(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12951(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12951.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 12951(b); no additional independent source was sought for this specific definition, and no case law applying it to particular facts was located or verified in this research session. The statute does not itself state which party bears the burden of proving or disproving business necessity in a dispute over a specific policy, and this clause does not resolve that question. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific business justification does or does not meet this three-part definition.

SECOND CONDITION: EMPLOYEES MUST BE NOTIFIED OF THE CIRCUMSTANCES AND CONSEQUENCES
The second of section 12951(a)'s two conditions is that the employer has notified its employees of the circumstances and the time when the language restriction is required to be observed, and of the consequences for violating it. Read together with the business necessity condition, the statute requires both a substantive justification for the restriction and a specific kind of advance communication about it -- when it applies and what happens if an employee does not comply -- before the restriction can be enforced consistent with this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(2) The employer has notified its employees of the circumstances and the time when the language
						restriction is required to be observed and of the consequences for violating the language restriction."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12951(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12951(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12951.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory paragraph, section 12951(a)(2). The raw HTML of the fetched leginfo page contains a line-wrap with embedded tab characters in the middle of this paragraph -- between the words "language" and "restriction" -- which this document's citation below reproduces exactly as fetched (verified in the raw HTML on two independent fetches) rather than silently smoothing over; it renders as ordinary whitespace in a browser. The statute's text does not specify a required form for this notice (written versus oral, a standalone notice versus inclusion in a handbook, or any particular lead time before the restriction takes effect), and this clause does not resolve those open questions -- no case law construing the notice requirement was located or verified in this research session.

WHICH EMPLOYERS SECTION 12951 REACHES: FEHA'S GENERAL "FIVE OR MORE" DEFINITION
Section 12951(a) applies to "an employer, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 12926" -- FEHA's own general definitions section, rather than a definition written specifically for section 12951. That definition states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, with one stated exception: "employer" does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(d) “Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  "“Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code § 12926(d), religious nonprofit exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926.)
  Known gap: This clause combines two citations that are not independent of one another: the cross-reference in section 12951(a) points directly to section 12926(d), and both are part of the same FEHA scheme within the same code. This clause states the statutory text only; it does not determine whether any specific business regularly employs five or more persons within the meaning of this definition, or whether any specific entity falls within the religious-association-or-nonprofit exception. This corpus separately relies on this same definition, section 12926(d), in other documents addressing different FEHA provisions that use the identical "employer" definition -- it is a single shared definitional source across those documents and this one, not independent corroboration for any of them.

SECTION 12951 SITS WITHIN FEHA'S CHAPTER ON DISCRIMINATION PROHIBITED
Government Code section 12951 is codified within Part 2.8 of the Government Code (the Civil Rights Department), Chapter 6 of that part -- captioned "Discrimination Prohibited" -- and within Article 1 of that chapter, captioned "Unlawful Practices, Generally," a span of sections running from 12940 to 12954. Section 12951's own text independently confirms this placement by describing a violation as "an unlawful employment practice," the same phrase FEHA's other unlawful-practices provisions use for conduct such as discriminatory refusal to hire or discharge.

  "ARTICLE 1. Unlawful Practices, Generally [12940 - 12954]"
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12951, chapter and article headings (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Article 1 heading as displayed for § 12951 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12951.)

It reflects the code structure only; it does not itself describe the Civil Rights Department's administrative complaint process or the civil-action route that generally applies to FEHA "unlawful employment practice" claims, which this research session did not independently verify for this specific section. This document does not determine that any specific enforcement mechanism, deadline, or remedy applicable to other FEHA provisions also applies to a section 12951 claim -- that determination was not made or verified here, and is disclosed as an open question rather than filled in with an assumption.

FEDERAL EEOC GUIDANCE DRAWS A RELATED, BUT NOT IDENTICAL, LINE
Separately from California law, a federal EEOC regulation addresses "speak-English-only" workplace rules under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. That regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7, does not track California's structure exactly: it distinguishes a rule applied "at all times," which the EEOC states it will presume violates Title VII and will closely scrutinize, from a rule applied "only at certain times," which the regulation states an employer may have where the employer can show the rule is justified by business necessity. For a certain-times rule, the regulation adds that if an employer believes it has a business necessity for the rule, the employer should inform its employees of the general circumstances when speaking only in English is required and of the consequences of violating the rule, and states that a failure to effectively notify employees, followed by an adverse action for a rule violation, will be considered by the EEOC as evidence of national-origin discrimination.

  "An employer may have a rule requiring that employees speak only in English at certain times where the employer can show that the rule is justified by business necessity."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7(b) (eCFR text), 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7(b), business-necessity standard for a rule applied at certain times (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1606/section-1606.7)
  "if an employer believes it has a business necessity for a speak-English-only rule at certain times, the employer should inform its employees of the general circumstances when speaking only in English is required and of the consequences of violating the rule. If an employer fails to effectively notify its employees of the rule and makes an adverse employment decision against an individual based on a violation of the rule, the Commission will consider the employer's application of the rule as evidence of discrimination on the basis of national origin."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7(c) (eCFR text), 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7(c), notice expectation and evidentiary consequence of a failure to notify (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XIV/part-1606/section-1606.7)

Unlike California's section 12951, which imposes its business-necessity-and-notice conditions on any policy that "limits or prohibits the use of any language," the EEOC regulation's business-necessity/notice framework by its own terms applies only to a rule applied "at certain times" -- a rule applied "at all times" is instead treated under a separate, stricter presumption in subdivision (a) of the regulation, a distinction California's statute does not draw in its own text. DESCRIPTION OF THE LANGUAGE-RELATED WORKPLACE POLICY
Acme, Inc. describes its language-related workplace policy, as it applies to Jordan Lee in the position of Retail Sales Associate, as follows: English only while operating the cash register during customer-facing transactions on the sales floor.

The stated business necessity for this policy, as Acme, Inc. understands the term used in California Government Code section 12951(b), is: so that a supervisor can verify price overrides and refund transactions in real time for loss-prevention purposes.

This description is provided for informational purposes in connection with the statutory requirements addressed elsewhere in this document. It is not itself a determination that this policy, as described, satisfies section 12951's business-necessity-and-notice conditions.

NOTICE TO EMPLOYEES OF CIRCUMSTANCES, TIMING, AND CONSEQUENCES
Acme, Inc. provides this notice to Jordan Lee effective November 1, 2026, addressing the two categories of information described in California Government Code section 12951(a)(2): the circumstances and time when the language restriction described elsewhere in this document is required to be observed, and the consequences of violating it.

Circumstances and timing: English only while operating the cash register during customer-facing transactions on the sales floor.

Consequences of a violation: as Acme, Inc. separately communicates in writing to Jordan Lee, consistent with Acme, Inc.'s generally applicable policies for workplace-rule violations.

This notice is a record of the communication described above; it is not itself a disciplinary action, and it does not state what action, if any, Acme, Inc. will take in response to any specific instance of noncompliance.

EMPLOYEE ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
I, Jordan Lee, acknowledge that I have received and reviewed the language-related workplace policy and notice described in this document from Acme, Inc., effective November 1, 2026. My signature below acknowledges receipt of this notice; it does not waive any right I may have under California Government Code section 12951 or any other law.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: September 6, 2026
